1.pericope_label: Hiram’s builders and cedar, David’s perception that the kingdom was confirmed, and the sons born at Jerusalem

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the Hebrew text of Chronicles spells the name Hiram, as do the Septuagint and all other ancient versions of both books, though the Hebrew margin here writes Huram; that messengers means ambassadors; that the cedar was felled in Lebanon and sea-borne to Joppa; and that the craftsmen are literally craftsmen of walls and craftsmen of timber, where Samuel has craftsmen of wood and craftsmen of stone of wall. The house he insists is a palace, the Temple being called the house as well as the palace, and he sets the project beside the records of palace building the Assyrian and Babylonian sovereigns left, cedar of Lebanon being a favourite material with them. He renders the next verse that David knew Jehovah had appointed him, finding the evidence in the embassy itself, and remarks that the favour of man is sometimes a sign of the approval of God, always so when it results from well-doing. Of the wives he observes the verse is considerably abbreviated against Samuel, which reads concubines and wives from Jerusalem after he had come from Hebron, the concubines not being omitted out of delicacy since they are named elsewhere in this book; and of the sons, that the list is repeated because it stood at this point in the document the historian copied, and perhaps as an instance of the prosperity which is the section’s topic, with Joseph tracing his descent from one of them. Keil and Delitzsch mark the difference from the older text, that where Samuel says Jehovah had lifted up his kingdom the Chronicle says his kingdom had been lifted up on high, the unusual form being probably a passive by contraction, and the phrase on high being here, as often in these books, a way of intensifying the expression.

Henry draws three lessons from the chapter’s opening. No man is of such sufficiency in himself that he has no need of his neighbours, for David had a very large kingdom and Hiram a very little one, yet David could not build himself a house to his mind unless Hiram furnished workmen and materials, a reason why we should despise none but be obliging to all. It is a satisfaction to a wise man to be settled and to a good man to see the special providences of God in his settlement, for the people had made David king but he could not be easy till he perceived that the Lord had confirmed him: who shall unfix me if God hath fixed me? And we must look on all our advancements as designed for usefulness, since the kingdom was lifted up not that David might look great but because of his people Israel, that he might be their guide and protector. Of the wives he allows the fault and then the blessing, that it is difficult to thrive without growing secure and indulgent to the flesh, and that it was David’s infirmity that on settling in his kingdom he took more wives, yet the numerous issue added to his honour and strength.

Clarke counts the names of the sons: in Samuel only eleven persons are named in the Hebrew, the Septuagint there has twenty-four, and here there are thirteen, all the versions agreeing in that number with varieties in the names. For the rest of the chapter’s opening he refers the reader to his notes on the parallel passage in Samuel.

debates.question: How many sons born at Jerusalem does the record give?

positions.view: Thirteen here, against eleven in the Hebrew of Samuel and twenty-four in the Septuagint there
The number is not the point; the list is repeated because it stood at that place in the source document, and as evidence of prosperity

outliers.claim: Alone in tracing the grammatical shift by which Chronicles turns Samuel’s active statement, that Jehovah lifted up the kingdom, into a passive one.
Alone in making the disparity between the two kings a lesson in mutual dependence, the large kingdom unable to build without the little one.

themes: Now Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and timber of cedars, with masons and carpenters, to build him an house
David perceived that the Lord had confirmed him king over Israel
his kingdom was lifted up on high, because of his people Israel
And David took more wives at Jerusalem: and David begat more sons and daughters
these are the names of his children which he had in Jerusalem

7.pericope_label: The Philistines spread in the valley of Rephaim, David enquires, smites them at Baal-perazim, and burns their gods

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the word all, omitted in Samuel, contrasts David’s second election with his first as king of Judah only; that to seek David means with hostile intent; and that where our text has he went out against them, literally before them, Samuel has he went down to the stronghold, a term used both of the castle of Zion and of David’s old refuge at Adullam in the valley of Elah, the latter probably intended, since the Philistines were likely to take that route. He explains how David enquired, through the high priest Abiathar, who sought divine direction by the Urim and Thummim, or sacred lots, carried in a pouch on his breast fastened to the ephod; and he corrects the punctuation, there being a comma and not a query after the word Philistines, the whole sentence forming one question in the Hebrew where Samuel gives two. At Baal-perazim he observes that it was David and his troops who came up, that the locality is unknown, and that Isaiah refers to these two victories together; that David, true to his character, owns the mighty hand of God in the results of his own valour, in contrast with the haughty self-confidence of the Assyrian conqueror; that the image of breaking waters is taken from the ground, the forces having probably charged down the slopes like a mountain torrent; and that the name means lord or owner of breaches, the plural perhaps also meaning the fissures on the mountain-side. Of the gods he notes that where Samuel says David and his men carried them off the chronicler says David gave a commandment and they were burned, the two not incompatible and perhaps both in the same original text, the chronicler being careful to record compliance with the law in Deuteronomy.

Henry takes the invasion as a warning that forbids us to be secure in any settlement and engages us to expect molestation in this world, for when we are most easy something may come to be a terror to us, and so Christ’s kingdom is insulted by the serpent’s seed, especially when it advances. David’s enquiring of God once and again should direct us in all our ways to acknowledge him: in distress to fly to him, when wronged to appeal to him, and when we know not what to do to ask counsel at his oracles. The victory he makes an encouragement to resist our spiritual enemies in observance of divine direction and dependence on divine strength, the devil resisted fleeing as the Philistines fled; and the burning of the gods he takes as instruction in a holy indignation against idolatry and all its remains.

Clarke contributes the Targum’s renderings at two points: that David consulted the Word of the Lord, and that the Lord had broken the enemies of David like the breaking of a potter’s vessel full of water. For the narrative itself he refers the reader to his notes on the parallel in Samuel.

outliers.claim: Alone in answering the question the text leaves open, how David enquired, by naming the high priest and the Urim and Thummim in their pouch on the ephod.
Alone in carrying the Targum into the chapter, which turns the breaking forth of waters into the breaking of a potter’s vessel.

themes: when the Philistines heard that David was anointed king over all Israel, all the Philistines went up to seek David
the Philistines came and spread themselves in the valley of Rephaim
David enquired of God, saying, Shall I go up against the Philistines? and wilt thou deliver them into mine hand?
God hath broken in upon mine enemies by mine hand like the breaking forth of waters: therefore they called the name of that place Baalperazim
when they had left their gods there, David gave a commandment, and they were burned with fire

13.pericope_label: The second invasion, the sound in the tops of the trees, the pursuit to Gazer, and the fame of David

schools.summary: Ellicott finds the first half of the verse about the second enquiry fuller and clearer here than in Samuel, but holds the second half must be adjusted by the older account, which reads: thou must not go up; go round to their rear, and come upon them in front of the baca trees; probably the terms rendered after them and from them should be modified and transposed. The mulberry trees he calls the traditional Jewish rendering of a Hebrew word occurring only here and in the parallel, taking them rather for the balsam tree the Arabs call baca, which sheds a gum like tears, whence its name. The sound he renders the sound of marching and allows the sign may have been natural, the wind rustling in the tops of the bacas like walking on dead leaves; he grants that all ancient peoples attached a prophetic import to rustling leaves, citing the great Assyrian work on terrestrial omens compiled by order of Sargon, the speaking oaks of Dodona, the laurel of Delos and that of Delphi, the oak of the diviners, perhaps the palm-tree of Deborah, and even the burning bush, as well as the Arab belief that certain thorny bushes utter prophetic words; and he insists these analogies do not militate against the reality or the miraculous character of the occurrence, since divine communications always take the form best adapted for striking the mind amidst reigning ideas, as the visions of Joseph are Egyptian and those of Ezekiel Assyrian. On the pursuit he notes the present Hebrew of Samuel has Geba while the Septuagint agrees with Chronicles in reading Gibeon, though the Targum and Syriac and Arabic read Geba; he prefers Gibeon, some six miles north-west of Jerusalem between the valley of Rephaim and Gezer, with Isaiah in support, and observes that Gazer is the pausal form of the name. The closing verse, he adds, is not in Samuel and looks like a concluding reflection of the chronicler’s: the fear of David was, as we should say, the natural effect of his victories, though in the chronicler’s view his success in arms with all its consequences was the work of Jehovah.

Clarke leaves nature out of the sign and gives the Targum: when thou shalt hear the sound of the angels coming to thy assistance, then go out to battle, for an angel is sent from the presence of God to render thy way prosperous. Of the closing verse he narrows the reach of the fame, that into all lands means all the surrounding or neighbouring lands and nations, for no others can possibly be intended.

debates.question: What was the sound in the tops of the trees?

positions.view: Possibly natural, the wind in the baca tops, and miraculous none the less, since revelation takes the form that strikes the mind of its age
The sound of angels coming to David’s assistance, as the Targum has it

debates.question: How far did David’s fame reach?

positions.view: All the lands, as the chronicler’s concluding reflection has it
Only the surrounding and neighbouring nations; no others can possibly be intended

outliers.claim: Alone in setting the rustling trees beside Assyrian omen-lists, Dodona, Delphi and the Arab sacred thorns, and then arguing that the parallels do not touch the miracle.

themes: the Philistines yet again spread themselves abroad in the valley
Go not up after them; turn away from them, and come upon them over against the mulberry trees
when thou shalt hear a sound of going in the tops of the mulberry trees, then thou shalt go out to battle
they smote the host of the Philistines from Gibeon even to Gazer
the fame of David went out into all lands; and the Lord brought the fear of him upon all nations
